podcast.title: Early Success with Artwork (1945)
podcast.body: Capitol Records released the King Cole Trio album in 1945, which spent most of a year at number one on the charts. This commercial success was a key factor in convincing the music industry of the significant value of album artwork in driving sales. "One of the biggest early successes was the King Cole trio. It was an album from that King Cole, issued by Capital Records in 1945. It was an old school album with 478 RPM records tucked into the sleeves. When it spent most of its year at number one on the charts, everybody was convinced about the value of artwork."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 2: Album Artwork

podcast.title: Acquisition by EMI (1955)
podcast.body: In 1955, Capitol Records was acquired by the large conglomerate EMI. This acquisition marked a turning point for the label, leading to changes in its direction and a new push towards embracing contemporary music styles. "However, in 1955 capital had been bought up by the big conglomerate EMI and things were changing at the label."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Search for an "Elvis Equivalent" (1955)
podcast.body: Despite Ken Nelson's lack of understanding of rockabilly, he recognized Capitol Records' need to find its own answer to Elvis Presley. He initiated a search for country singers who could emulate Elvis, which eventually led to him calling in Gene Vincent for a session after receiving a tape from Tex Davis. "Nelson didn't really understand rock-a-billy at all, but he knew that capital needed its own equivalent of Elvis Presley, so he put out a call for people to recommend him country singers who could sound a bit like Elvis..."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: New Hollywood Studio (1957)
podcast.body: Capitol Records opened a new recording studio located in the Capitol Tower in Hollywood. This facility became the site where Gene Vincent recorded his song "Lotta Lovin'." "Lotta Lovein was quickly recorded at Jean's first session at Capital's new studio at the Capital Tower in Hollywood."

podcast.title: Recall of "Butcher Cover" Album (1966)
podcast.body: Capitol Records, The Beatles' American record label, immediately recalled all 60,000 copies of "Yesterday and Today" with the "Butcher Cover" that had been sent to stores in 1966, and held back an additional 750,000 records in warehouses due to the controversial artwork. "Capital records, the band's American record label, immediately recalled all 60,000 albums that had been sent out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Valuable Vinyl

podcast.title: First Song Sold Online (1997)
podcast.body: Capitol Records pioneered digital music sales in 1997 by issuing Duran Duran's "Electric Barbarella" as a 99-cent digital single. This marked the first song sold online, three years after the first free distribution, although it was released in a now "long defunct format called Liquid Audio," indicating its beta test nature. "Durand Durand's minor 1997 hit Electric Barbarella, a number 52 hot 100 hit, was issued by Capital Records as a 99 cent digital single."

podcast.title: "Incomprehensible Decisions" in Artist Management (Early 1960s)
podcast.body: Capitol Records made several "incomprehensible decisions" regarding The Beach Boys' early releases. A notable example was following up their initial national hit "Surf and Safari" with an album track, "Ten Little Indians," as a single. This choice proved commercially unsuccessful, with the song only reaching number 49 on the charts. "When we left the beach boys, they had just secured a contract with capital records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 117: "Don't Worry Baby" by the Beach Boys

podcast.title: "Optical Center" 45 RPM Adapter
podcast.body: Capitol Records took inspiration from Fidelatone's adapter design to create their own solution called the "optical center." This adapter was a triangular piece of cardboard built into the big hole of a 45, covering most of the open space but leaving a central hole for an LP spindle. It could be punched out but not reinserted. "But then capital records took the Fidelatone idea and created an adapter that they called the optical center that was built into the big hole."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 3

podcast.title: Acetates Used for Fake Production Credits
podcast.body: Shell Tauhmey, an engineer seeking work in the UK, was given a stack of acetates of "recent capital records" produced by Nick Vennett. Tauhmey then presented these, claiming he produced them, to Dick Rowe at Decca Records to secure a job, including "Surf and Safari" by The Beach Boys and "Music in the Air" by Lou Rawls. "Vennett gave him a stack of acetates of recent capital records that he produced, and told him that he could pretend to produce them if he got in work."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Consequences of *Paul's Boutique*'s Commercial Failure
podcast.body: The initial dismal sales of *Paul's Boutique* were such a significant commercial failure that the president of Capitol Records was fired for allowing the band to be signed to the label, and his was "not the only head that rolled." "It was such a stiff that the president of capital was fired for allowing the band to be signed to the label."

podcast.title: Copy Protection Controversy
podcast.body: In Europe, Capitol Records, the Beastie Boys' label, utilized MacroVision CDS2000, a copy protection software on "To the 5 Boroughs" CDs. While it didn't install malware like the Sony rootkit, its resemblance to a virus caused controversy and problems for the band. "In Europe, capital records, the Beastie's label, used something called MacroVision CDS2000, which was a rather insidious form of copy protection software that mimicked a virus."

podcast.title: Distribution Partner for "Reflektor"
podcast.body: Capitol Records, a division of the Universal Music Empire, entered into a "Back in Services" agreement with Arcade Fire for the release of their "Reflektor" album. This deal provided the independent band with the extensive distribution, promotion, and marketing capabilities typically offered by a major label, crucial for the album's broad reach. "First, they struck a deal with capital records, which is part of the Universal Music Empire."

podcast.title: Fastest-Selling Album Record
podcast.body: Capitol Records released The Knack's debut record, which became its fastest-selling album since The Beatles' "Meet the Beatles" in 1964. This achievement highlights the immense commercial success of The Knack's Powerpop sound. "The Nack's debut record, which hit number one in both Canada and the US, was the fastest-selling album Capital Records released since Meet the Beatles in 1964."

podcast.title: Founding and Early Focus (Early 1940s)
podcast.body: Capitol Records was established in the early 1940s by songwriter Johnny Mercer, who wrote many standards for artists like Frank Sinatra, Bing Crosby, and Tony Bennett. The label initially served as a home for these traditional artists, and aside from a small country music division, it largely lacked engagement with the emerging new forms of music such as rock and roll. "Karl had been founded in the early 1940s by the songwriter Johnny Mercer... Capital at the time was the home of crew members like Frank Sinatra and Nat King Cole..."

podcast.title: Historic Recording Studio
podcast.body: Capitol Records' studio in Los Angeles holds significant historical importance, notably as the place where The Beach Boys recorded their landmark album "Pet Sounds." Happy Mondays also chose this studio to record their "Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches" album. "The studio that did Pet Sounds in a Found Outlay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of "Madchester" - Part 1

podcast.title: Ken Nelson's Role and Reputation
podcast.body: Ken Nelson served as the head of country music for Capitol Records. He held a "very mixed reputation" among music lovers: praised for his "impeccable taste in artists," demonstrated by signing Buck Owens and The Louvin Brothers, but criticized for his tendency to impose styles on artists that didn't suit them, and a general misunderstanding of rockabilly. "Ben Nelson was the head of country music for capital records and is someone who has a very mixed reputation among lovers of both country music and rock-a-billy..."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Lack of Rock and Roll Understanding
podcast.body: Capitol Records, particularly through the decisions of Ken Nelson, displayed a notable lack of understanding regarding rock and roll music. This was evidenced by their suggestions for Gene Vincent to record unsuitable "old standards," which contributed to his struggle to gain lasting success in the US. "Capital and Ken Nelson's lack of understanding of rock and roll music meant that he quickly became a forgotten figure in the US."

podcast.title: Luther Dixon's Post-Scepter Employment
podcast.body: After Luther Dixon and Florence Greenberg ended their professional and personal relationship, Dixon moved on to a new job at Capitol Records. "Dixon and Greenberg ended their relationship, and Dixon went on to a new job at Capital Records."

podcast.title: New Wave Profitability
podcast.body: Capitol Records experienced astounding profits from The Knack's 1979 debut album, "Get The Knack," which became their fastest-selling debut since "Meet the Beatles" and fastest-selling single since "I Want to Hold Your Hand," demonstrating the significant financial returns possible from investing in New Wave bands. "The profit realized by capital on the NAC was astounding."

podcast.title: Nick Vene's Influence
podcast.body: Nick Vene (Nick Renee) secured a job at Capitol Records. He used his position, along with owning the master tape and publishing rights for The Gamblers' "Moon Dog," to place the song on the Capitol compilation album "Golden Gasses," significantly broadening its audience despite its initial minor success. "Vene had taken a job at capital records. And Vene doing that suddenly meant that Mundoag became very important indeed."

podcast.title: President Fired for Paul's Boutique
podcast.body: The commercial failure of the Beastie Boys' album "Paul's Boutique" was so significant that the president of Capitol Records was fired for allowing the band to be signed to the label, indicating a major misjudgment by the label at the time. "It was such a stiff that the president of Capital was fired for allowing the band to be signed to the label."

podcast.title: Producer Ken Nelson
podcast.body: Ken Nelson was the producer at Capitol Records who was initially approached by Hank Thompson with demos of a teenage Wanda Jackson. Nelson liked her voice but declined to sign her due to her age and legal complications. Later, after Jackson had turned 18, Thompson revisited Nelson, who then signed her to Capitol Tower. Nelson produced Jackson's recordings, including "I Gotta Know," utilizing West Coast session musicians. However, he also made mistakes in selecting material for Jackson, similar to his issues with Gene Vincent, often choosing songs that failed to connect with audiences.

podcast.title: Signing The Stone Poneys
podcast.body: Capitol Records signed Linda Ronstadt and her band, The Stone Poneys, to a record deal shortly after their two-week gig at The Troubadour in 1965. "And then they got her record deal with capital records not long after that."

podcast.title: Signing the Beastie Boys and Creative Freedom (Late 1980s)
podcast.body: Capitol Records signed the Beastie Boys after their contentious departure from Def Jam, offering the group "total freedom" in making their next album. However, the label was expecting a commercial success akin to *Licensed to Ill* but instead received *Paul's Boutique*, an unexpected and commercially challenging record. "But capital was expecting another license to yield. What they got was something unexpected and something very ahead of its time."
